# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the management of severe aortic stenosis across the surgical-risk spectrum, beginning with inoperable and high-risk patients in the landmark PARTNER trials. In patients with severe aortic stenosis who were not suitable candidates for surgery, transcatheter aortic-valve implantation, as compared with standard therapy, significantly reduced the rates of death from any cause, despite a higher incidence of major strokes and major vascular events. [1] These complications drew early attention to the importance of vascular access, since the large-bore sheaths required for transcatheter heart valves demand suitably sized delivery vessels [2].

The transfemoral route remains the default approach. However, despite improvement in device profiles and procedural techniques, femoral peripheral access cannot be performed in approximately 10% to 15% of patients due to iliofemoral arteriopathy, tortuosity, severe calcifications, aortic aneurysm, mural thrombus, or previous vascular surgery. [3] Historically, such patients were offered transthoracic (transapical or transaortic) access or referred for surgery, although these approaches carry meaningful morbidity [4,5]. Transcaval access emerged to address this gap.

## Concept and Rationale

Transcaval aortic access is a versatile electrosurgical technique for large-bore arterial access through the wall of the abdominal aorta from the adjoining inferior vena cava. [6] Although it seems paradoxical to deliberately puncture the aorta from the cava, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole. [6] The approach builds on principles of transcatheter electrosurgery, in which radiofrequency energy is used to traverse tissue planes despite flowing blood [7]. Preclinical work established feasibility of caval-to-aortic crossing for large-caliber devices before its translation to humans [8].

## Technique

In practice, an electrified guidewire is directed from the femoral vein and inferior vena cava across the retroperitoneal space into the infrarenal aorta, typically captured by a pre-positioned aortic snare [9]. In the pivotal prospective study, 100 patients underwent attempted percutaneous transcaval access to the abdominal aorta by electrifying a caval guidewire and advancing it into a pre-positioned aortic snare. [10] After valve delivery, the aortocaval tract is closed, most commonly with off-label nitinol cardiac occluders, although purpose-built closure devices have since been developed [11,12]. Candidate selection relies on computed tomography: candidates need a calcium-free window on the caval side of the aorta, away from important arterial branches, with no interposed viscera, within reach of an available TAVR introducer sheath. [13]

## Clinical Outcomes

The first human experience demonstrated that caval-aortic access could enable TAVR in otherwise ineligible patients [14]. In the subsequent prospective trial, transcaval access enabled TAVR in patients who were not good candidates for transthoracic access; bleeding and vascular complications, using permeable nitinol cardiac occluders to close the access ports, were common but acceptable in this high-risk cohort. [10] At one year, results were reassuring: there were no late vascular complications of transcaval access, and 93% of fistulas were proven occluded at last follow-up. [15] CT demonstrated spontaneous closure of almost all fistulas. [15]

European experience corroborated these findings. Transcaval access proved to be a feasible and safe alternative TAVI access strategy for high-risk patients with severe aortic stenosis not suitable for a transfemoral and transaxillary/subclavian access. [16] A comprehensive best-practices document has since codified the technique, noting that transcaval access has been performed in thousands of patients for transcatheter aortic valve replacement and endovascular thoracic aneurysm repair and to avoid limb ischemia in percutaneous mechanical circulatory support. [17]

## Comparative Data

A key question is how transcaval access compares with other nonfemoral routes. In a propensity-weighted analysis, transcaval access had a low transfemoral-like stroke rate, an increased transaxillary-like bleeding rate, and transfemoral-like favorable operator ergonomics and radiation exposure. [18] Stroke/transient ischemic attack rates were 3% for transcaval and 13% for transaxillary TAVR. [18] However, patients undergoing nonfemoral access had worse outcomes than those undergoing transfemoral access, including worse bleeding, vascular complications, stroke or TIA, and mortality. [18] Broader registry data similarly show that nonfemoral peripheral TAVR is associated with similar outcomes compared with femoral TAVR, except for a 2-fold lower rate of major vascular complications and unplanned vascular repairs favoring femoral access. [19] Single-centre and meta-analytic comparisons of transfemoral, transcarotid, and transcaval routes have generally found broadly comparable survival [20,21,22], and supra-aortic comparisons suggest neurovascular complications may be lower with transcaval access [22].

## Applications Beyond TAVR

Transcaval access has expanded beyond aortic valve therapy. It has been described for thoracic endovascular aortic repair when iliofemoral vessels are inadequate: in a 61-year-old man with a descending thoracic aneurysm, transcaval access was performed in lieu of a surgical iliac conduit in view of small atherosclerotic pelvic arteries, and TEVAR was successfully performed, followed by intervascular tract occlusion. [23,24] It has also been used to deliver mechanical circulatory support: transcaval access is feasible for emergency nonsurgical implantation of the Impella 5.0 device in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries. [25] The shared electrosurgical platform also underpins adjunctive leaflet-modification procedures such as BASILICA, which prevents coronary obstruction and is frequently performed via nonfemoral access [26,27,28]. Reported series further demonstrate feasibility in challenging populations including morbidly obese patients [29] and in bicuspid anatomy [30].

## Limitations and Future Directions

Important limitations persist. The main disadvantage of transcaval access is higher material costs for the closure device and deflectable sheath, longer fluoroscopy time and contrast dose, and less well-disseminated operator experience. [18] The dissemination of transcaval access and closure techniques has been hampered by the unavailability of commercially marketed devices. [17] As sheath profiles shrink and transfemoral eligibility broadens, the absolute number of patients requiring alternative access continues to decline [3,16]. Nonetheless, for the minority with prohibitive iliofemoral disease, transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous alternative with transfemoral-like ergonomics and a favorable stroke profile, and dedicated closure devices may further improve safety [12,17].
